Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Mateo Rivera was twenty-one when the roof access door gave way. He had been hauling a cast-iron pump housing up the narrow service ladder, the heavy metal pressing against his ribs. His mentor, Silas, was ahead of him, steadying the guide rail. Mateo had just shifted his weight to brace the load when the rungs buckled beneath his boot. There was a sharp crack, then the sound of a man falling through two stories of ductwork. When Mateo crept to the edge, Silas was lying still in a tangle of insulation, clutching his back. The air still carried the sharp tang of hot compressor oil and scorched rubber. Mateo had called 911 before his hands would stop trembling, but the silence that followed the paramedic’s radio chatter made his chest tighten, as if the quiet itself were waiting for another collapse. The memory never settled neatly into his mind. Some afternoons, when he closed his eyes, it felt like footage from a stranger’s tape recorder. He would catch himself staring at his own hands, certain they no longer belonged to him. The person who used to laugh with his abuela’s friends at Sunday parrilladas was gone, replaced by someone who flinched at the slightest metallic clank. He replayed the ladder’s failure a hundred times a night, tracing the exact angle of his foot, the precise moment his grip slipped, certain he would never forgive himself for not doing more the moment Silas fell. He carried a heavy certainty that his own body had turned against him, that the muscles he once relied on had simply stopped working when he needed them most. Over the following months, Mateo’s daily landscape shifted. He found that only his bedroom, with the deadbolt thrown and the blinds drawn, kept his breathing steady. Anything that felt remotely stressful—scheduling a double shift, returning a call from his foreman, even the sudden hush of an empty kitchen—coexisted with a familiar rush of panic. His heart would hammer against his ribs, his palms would slicken, and the smell of hot oil would ghost through his nose out of nowhere. The memory forces its way into his mind when he does not want to, interrupting routine thermostat calibrations and quiet drives alike. He started turning down overtime, canceling plans, and carefully sidestepping the anniversary of the date Silas went to the hospital. The avoidance became a quiet routine. He told himself it was just being careful, but the days bled into months of withdrawal. His days and his work occupied the same space. As an HVAC technician, Mateo spent his hours climbing into attics and balancing on commercial rooftops, his job depending on steady hands and sharp awareness. When his foreman asked him to lead a complex condenser replacement, Mateo’s throat closed. He could not stop hearing the ladder’s groan, nor could he shake the certainty that his arms would fail him again on a high roof. He declined the assignment, then began skipping the mandatory pre-job safety checks, leaving the checklist blank and walking out of the site. His supervisor finally sat him down, explaining that his recent absences and hesitation were putting client safety at risk. Mateo nodded, swallowing the familiar shame, but he could not bring himself to climb the next service ladder. Now twenty-two and single, Mateo sits on the edge of his mattress, the phone between his thighs, watching the screen dim. He has finally scheduled an intake, drawn by the realization that the quiet moments at work no longer just make him anxious—they make him feel like he is losing his footing in his own life. He does not know if a therapist can untangle the guilt that tells him he will never forgive himself for not acting faster, or help him believe that a body can be trusted again. He only knows that the silence is getting harder to endure, and he is tired of waiting for the next thing to fall.
